newsitem.title: MEXICO: Televisa has solid 96 oper net - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Televisa has solid 96 oper net - analysts.

text.p: Media giant Televisa posted solid operating results in 1996 and reported its first quarterly net gain in more than a year, analysts said on Monday, adding to relief about a management overhaul.

"I think they were excellent results on an operating basis," said Marla Marron, media specialist at ING Barings in New York. "Operating cash flow was up 36 percent in the year and 30 percent in the fourth quarter."
Televisa reported a 1996 0.9 peso share loss late Monday, compared with a profit of 1.02 pesos the year before. Analysts said the loss was due to extraordinary items and a weak start to the year.
Sales in 1996 grew to 11.513 billion pesos from 11.283 billion pesos in 1995, and operating income grew to 1.042 billion pesos from 630.7 million over the same period.

"Top-offs were better than expected," Marron said, adding that the fourth quarter continued to reflect the benefits of a cost-reduction program. "Also, on a relative basis, they were not as hurt by the exchange rate."
Top-offs are advertising revenues received by Televisa in addition to so-called "French Plan" payments deposited in advance in return for advertising discounts.

Martin Lara of Caspian Research said there was an increase of some 4.5 percent in advertising at Televisa last year that helped push up revenues, and that in the fourth quarter sales from the firm's television unit, partly via direct-to-home television, jumped 22 percent.
"Television sales were especially strong in the fourth quarter," he said.

In the final three months of last year, he said, Televisa reported its first profit in five quarters, or 172 million pesos compared to a loss of 111 million pesos in Q4 1995, when Mexico's economic crisis was in full swing.
Operating margins, he said, were 16.9 percent last quarter, compared with 12.9 percent in the same quarter the previous year and 10.1 percent in Q3 1996.
"There's a very strong operating leverage. They have a fixed cost structure so any increase in sales produces much better margins," he said.
He expected Televisa's advertising market to grow some 20 percent in 1997.

A stronger economy is expected to boost advertising revenues, as are windfall gains from the publicity battles in the long-distance telephone market, private pension funds and in campaigns ahead of mid-term elections in July.

Televisa shares surged on Tuesday in both Mexico and New York, partly because of the results and partly because the market accepted the resignation on Monday of the company's long-time chairman Emilio Azcarraga Milmo.

Lara said the management switch was positive because Azcarraga will be succeeded by his son Emilio Azcarraga Jean as president and chief operating officer, and by Guillermo Canedo White as chairman and chief corporate officer.
Those positions play to their strengths, he said, Canedo White as a financial planner and Azcarraga Jean as a programmer.

Marron said the resignation of Azcarraga Milmo was "obviously not ideal", describing him as a visionary who may leave a void in terms of seeing the future of Mexican television. He has led Televisa for more than two decades.

But she expected little disruption to the firm over the next 3-5 years, because he had put his two top aides on the path that he wanted them to follow, and they would be kept busy by the growth of direct-to-home TV.
"I'm not worried about (the change) on an operating basis. The question is will they have the same vision? I don't know," she said.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9569))
